info.text: Right-of-way, stopped school buses, and assured clear distance. Items map one to one onto the Unit 4 Lesson checkpoints.

name.text: U04-Q01 Behind a stopped school bus on a four-lane road

questiontext.text:
You are on a four-lane road, driving behind a school bus in the same direction it is travelling. The bus stops and its red lights begin flashing.

What are you required to do?

generalfeedback.text: The four-lane exception in R.C. 4511.75 applies only to a driver meeting the bus from the opposite direction. Travelling the same direction, you stop at least ten feet from the bus and stay stopped until it moves or the driver signals you on.

answer.text: Stop at least ten feet behind the bus and wait until it moves or the driver signals you on.

feedback.text: Yes. Nothing in the statute cancels this duty for a driver behind the bus, whatever the lane count.

answer.text: Slow down and pass with caution, because the road has four or more lanes.

feedback.text: The lane count is a real test, but you only reach it when you are meeting the bus from the opposite direction.

answer.text: Change lanes and continue at normal speed, since another lane is open.

feedback.text: An open lane changes nothing. The duty attaches to the stopped bus and its flashing red lights.

answer.text: Stop only if you can see children crossing in front of the bus.

feedback.text: The trigger is the stopped bus with red lights flashing. You usually cannot see the child from behind, which is why the rule does not depend on seeing one.

name.text: U04-Q02 Meeting a stopped school bus on a two-lane road

questiontext.text:
A two-lane road, one lane in each direction. A school bus stops ahead of you in the oncoming lane with its red lights flashing.

What are you required to do?

generalfeedback.text: Travelling the opposite direction gets you to the lane question, not past it. R.C. 4511.75 excuses a meeting driver only on a highway of four or more traffic lanes. Two lanes is fewer than four, so you stop.

answer.text: Stop at least ten feet away and wait for the bus to move or the driver to signal you on.

feedback.text: Yes. The exception needs four or more lanes, and this road has two.

answer.text: Proceed with caution, because you are travelling the opposite direction.

feedback.text: Direction is the first question, not the only one. Count the lanes before you decide.

answer.text: Continue at normal speed, because the bus is not in your lane.

feedback.text: On a two-lane road a child crossing to the far side crosses your lane. That is the case the rule exists for.

name.text: U04-Q03 Ten feet, and staying stopped

questiontext.text: A driver required to stop for a school bus may start moving again as soon as the last child is off the road, even if the bus still has its red lights flashing.

generalfeedback.text: False. Under R.C. 4511.75 you stop at least ten feet from the front or rear of the bus and stay stopped until the bus resumes motion or the bus driver signals you to proceed. Judging for yourself that the crossing is finished is not one of the two releases.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: No. Two things release you: the bus moves, or the driver signals you on.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Right. You wait for the bus to move or for the driver to wave you through.

name.text: U04-Q04 Assured clear distance in fog

questiontext.text:
The posted limit is 55 mph. Dense fog cuts visibility to roughly 100 feet. You are driving 52 mph and you strike a car stopped in your lane.

Can you be cited for your speed?

generalfeedback.text: Yes. R.C. 4511.21 forbids driving faster than will permit stopping within the assured clear distance ahead. When visibility falls, the lawful speed falls with it, whatever the sign says.

answer.text: Yes. Assured clear distance sets a lower lawful speed than the posted limit when you cannot see far ahead.

feedback.text: Yes. At 100 feet of visibility the question is whether you could stop in 100 feet, and at 52 mph you could not.

answer.text: No. You were under the posted limit, so your speed was lawful.

feedback.text: The posted number is a maximum for good conditions. It does not make every lower speed lawful.

answer.text: No. The driver who stopped in a travel lane caused the crash.

feedback.text: Whatever that driver did, the duty to be able to stop inside the distance you can see is yours.

answer.text: Only if the fog had been reported in advance.

feedback.text: Nothing in the statute waits on a report. The conditions in front of you are the conditions.

name.text: U04-Q05 The posted limit as a ceiling

questiontext.text: Driving at or below the posted speed limit means your speed is always lawful.

generalfeedback.text: False. Two limits are in force at once: the posted maximum, and the speed that lets you stop within the assured clear distance ahead under R.C. 4511.21. The lower of the two governs.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: No. Fog, ice, a blind crest or a stopped car can each put the lawful speed below the sign.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Right. The sign is a ceiling for good conditions, not a permission for all of them.

questiontext.text:
At an intersection with no signs or signals you are the vehicle on the right, travelling 45 mph in a 25 mph zone. A car arrives from your left at about the same moment and the two of you collide.

Being on the right put the other driver in the yielding position. What does that mean for you?

generalfeedback.text: R.C. 4511.01 defines right-of-way as the right to proceed uninterruptedly in a lawful manner. Ohio courts have held that a driver keeps preferred-party status unless that driver violated a legal requirement. Speeding is the common one, so the preference is not safe here.

answer.text: You can lose the preference, because Ohio attaches right-of-way to proceeding in a lawful manner and 45 in a 25 is not lawful.

feedback.text: Yes. The definition and the speed rule meet here.

answer.text: You keep the right-of-way, because the rule is about position and not speed.

feedback.text: Position decides who yields. Lawful movement decides whether the preference survives.

answer.text: The right-of-way rule does not apply without signs or signals.

feedback.text: An uncontrolled intersection is exactly where the vehicle-on-the-right rule does its work.

answer.text: You keep the right-of-way and the two drivers share the penalty.

feedback.text: Right-of-way is not divided. Each driver is measured against what the law required of that driver.

name.text: U04-Q07 After the stop at a stop sign

questiontext.text:
You come to a complete stop at a stop sign. A car on the through street is approaching, close enough that pulling out would force it to brake hard.

What does Ohio law require next?

generalfeedback.text: Stopping and yielding are two duties, not one. Under R.C. 4511.43, after stopping you must still yield to traffic already in the intersection and to traffic approaching so closely as to constitute an immediate hazard.

answer.text: Wait, and yield to the approaching car, because it is close enough to be an immediate hazard.

feedback.text: Yes. The stop satisfies one duty; yielding is the other.

answer.text: Proceed, because you stopped first and that gives you the right-of-way.

feedback.text: Arriving first does not transfer the preference to the driver facing the stop sign.

answer.text: Proceed slowly, so the other driver has time to react.

feedback.text: Making the other driver adjust is the definition of failing to yield.

answer.text: Proceed if you can clear the intersection before the other car reaches it.

feedback.text: The test is whether the approaching vehicle is an immediate hazard, not whether you can beat it.
